title: TAMAR WAS PASSED BETWEEN MEN WHILE HER FUTURE WAS BEING DECIDED FOR HER
paragraphs:
TAMAR WAS PASSED BETWEEN MEN WHILE HER FUTURE WAS BEING DECIDED FOR HER
She buried one husband. Then another man used what should have protected her for his own advantage. Then the man who promised her a future quietly left her waiting for one he never intended to give. But God was watching the woman everyone else had placed on hold.
There is a kind of pain that comes from losing someone.
And then there is another kind.
The pain of realizing that while you were grieving, other people were making decisions about your life as though your heart were not even in the room.
Tamar knew something about that pain.
Her story in Genesis 38 is uncomfortable.
Not uncomfortable because Scripture is careless with morality, but because Scripture refuses to sanitize what human sin actually does to people.
Tamar enters the biblical narrative almost without introduction.
No childhood.
No long description.
No recorded conversation about what she wanted.
Just one sentence:
“Judah got a wife for Er his first-born; her name was Tamar.”
In Hebrew:
וּשְׁמָהּ תָּמָר
U-shemah Tamar.
“Her name was Tamar.”
Her name.
Remember that.
Because before this chapter is finished, men will make decisions affecting her marriage, her widowhood, her motherhood, her security, and potentially her survival.
But God never forgets her name.
Judah chooses Tamar as a wife for his firstborn son, Er.
Then Scripture gives a terrifyingly brief judgment on Er: he was wicked in the sight of the LORD, and the LORD put him to death.
We are not told here exactly what Er did.
That matters.
We should never accuse a biblical character of sins the Bible itself does not identify.
What Scripture does tell us is enough.
Tamar became a widow.
Imagine the silence after that.
Whatever expectations she carried into that marriage disappeared.
Whatever future she imagined was buried.
And in the social world surrounding the text, widowhood could mean far more than loneliness. Marriage, offspring, household belonging, inheritance, and economic security were deeply connected.
Tamar had lost more than a husband.
Her future had become uncertain.
Then Judah spoke to his second son, Onan.
The Hebrew of Genesis 38:8 is striking:
בֹּא אֶל־אֵשֶׁת אָחִיךָ וְיַבֵּם אֹתָהּ וְהָקֵם זֶרַע לְאָחִיךָ
Bo el-eshet achikha, veyabbem otah, vehakem zera le-achikha.
In sense:
Go to your brother’s wife, perform your brother-in-law duty toward her, and raise up offspring for your brother.
The verb behind this duty is connected with yibbum, the brother-in-law obligation later formally addressed in Deuteronomy 25:5–10.
The purpose was not simply sexual access.
It concerned family continuity.
Name.
Offspring.
Responsibility.
Protection within the covenant community.
But Onan knew something.
The text says:
וַיֵּדַע אוֹנָן כִּי לֹּא לוֹ יִהְיֶה הַזָּרַע
Vayyeda Onan ki lo lo yihyeh hazzara.
“Onan knew that the offspring would not be his.”
And suddenly the ugliness becomes clearer.
Onan wanted something from the arrangement without accepting the responsibility attached to it.
Genesis says that when he went in to Tamar, he deliberately prevented conception because he did not want to provide offspring for his brother.
Do not rush past that.
Tamar had already buried one husband.
Now another man repeatedly entered the relationship while intentionally denying the very outcome his obligation was supposed to provide.
The biblical issue is larger than the simplistic way this passage is sometimes discussed.
The text itself emphasizes his refusal to provide offspring for his brother.
He accepted intimacy while sabotaging responsibility.
He participated physically while withholding covenant duty.
And God saw it.
Genesis says what Onan did was evil in the sight of the LORD.
The LORD put him to death also.
And Tamar became a widow again.
Two husbands.
Two funerals.
No child.
No secure future.
Then Judah spoke.
Perhaps these words initially sounded like hope:
“Stay as a widow in your father’s house until my son Shelah grows up.”
Wait.
Just wait.
There is another son.
There is still a future.
There is still a possibility.
But the narrator lets us hear what Tamar could not hear.
Judah was afraid.
He thought Shelah might die like his brothers.
And so Tamar was sent away.
Genesis says:
שְׁבִי אַלְמָנָה בֵית־אָבִיךְ
Shevi almanah beit-avikh.
“Remain a widow in your father’s house.”
And she did.
That sentence hurts differently when you have ever been told to wait by someone who had no intention of keeping their promise.
Wait until things improve.
Wait until I am ready.
Wait until the timing is right.
Wait until they change.
Wait until someone finally chooses you.
Tamar waited.
Shelah grew.
And still Tamar was not given to him.
That detail changes everything.
She was not simply impatient.
Genesis explicitly tells us that Tamar saw Shelah had grown up and that she had not been given to him.
The promised future had arrived.
The promise had not.
There are people reading this who know that particular wound.
Not Tamar’s exact circumstances.
But the feeling.
Someone else controlled the decision.
Someone else held the authority.
Someone else made the promise.
And you were left living inside the consequences.
Maybe someone abandoned you and continued living as though nothing happened.
Maybe somebody used your vulnerability while calling it love.
Maybe a person kept you close enough to benefit from you but never close enough to honor you.
Maybe you were told to wait.
And wait.
And wait.
Until one day you realized you were not waiting for circumstances to change.
You were waiting for someone to become honest.
Tamar eventually stopped waiting.
What happens next is one of the Bible’s most morally complicated family scandals.
After Judah’s wife died and his period of mourning passed, Tamar learned that Judah was traveling toward Timnah for the sheep shearing.
She removed her widow’s garments.
She covered herself with a veil.
She positioned herself along his route.
Judah saw her and assumed she was a prostitute.
He did not recognize his own daughter-in-law.
He propositioned her.
Tamar asked what he would give her.
Judah promised a young goat.
But Tamar wanted collateral.
“What pledge will you give me?”
His seal.
His cord.
His staff.
In that world, these were not meaningless trinkets.
They were identifying objects.
Tamar did not merely obtain payment.
She obtained evidence.
Judah slept with her.
She conceived.
Then she left, removed the veil, and put the garments of her widowhood back on.
And approximately three months later, the scandal exploded.
Judah was told that Tamar had become pregnant through sexual immorality.
His response was horrifyingly swift.
“Bring her out.”
Judgment came quickly from a man who had been remarkably slow to examine himself.
Then Tamar did something extraordinary.
She did not scream.
She did not deliver a long accusation.
She sent the evidence.
The seal.
The cord.
The staff.
And essentially said:
Identify these.
Whose are they?
There is an almost poetic justice here.
The man prepared to expose Tamar publicly was forced to recognize himself privately.
Judah looked.
He knew.
And then Genesis records one of the most important confessions in the entire story:
צָדְקָה מִמֶּנִּי
Tzadqah mimmeni.
“She is more righteous than I.”
Or, in context, “She is more in the right than I.”
Then Judah explains why:
Because he had not given Tamar to Shelah.
There it is.
The truth finally spoken aloud.
Judah acknowledges his failure.
This does not mean Scripture is declaring every action Tamar took an ideal model for Christian ethics.
Genesis is narrating an ancient and deeply broken situation, not issuing Christians a command to imitate every decision within it.
But neither does Scripture allow us to turn Judah into an innocent observer.
His own confession identifies the injustice.
“I did not give her to my son Shelah.”
Tamar had been waiting inside a future Judah had promised but withheld.
And now the man prepared to condemn her discovered that his own failure was sitting in her hands.
Maybe that is where this story becomes dangerous to religious people.
Because we are often very good at seeing the visible scandal.
God sees the hidden chain of decisions that preceded it.
We see the pregnancy.
God saw the waiting.
We see Tamar by the road.
God saw Tamar sent home.
We see the disguise.
God saw the broken promise.
We see the moment everybody whispers about.
God sees the years nobody asks about.
That does not make sin righteous.
It means righteous judgment requires truth.
And this is where Genesis 38 begins reaching beyond Tamar.
Because some of us have become experts at judging the chapter of somebody’s life we happened to walk into while knowing nothing about the chapters that came before it.
We see the breakdown but not the betrayal.
The anger but not the wound.
The addiction but not the emptiness.
The divorce but not the years behind closed doors.
The coldness but not the abandonment.
The church absence but not what happened inside the church.
The scandal but not the suffering.
Again, pain does not make every response right.
Victimhood does not transform sin into holiness.
The Gospel never requires us to rename darkness as light.
But neither does Jesus teach us to become self-righteous spectators who throw stones while refusing to examine our own hearts.
Because eventually every one of us comes to the same terrifying place Judah reached.
The evidence points back at us.
Not Tamar’s evidence.
Ours.
Our pride.
Our lust.
Our bitterness.
Our deception.
Our selfishness.
Our secret compromises.
Our carefully edited Christianity.
Our private browser histories.
Our resentment.
Our unforgiveness.
Our hunger to appear righteous instead of becoming holy.
Our tendency to condemn publicly what we secretly excuse privately.
And before the holiness of God, none of us survives by saying, “At least I am better than Tamar.”
We survive only by grace.
That is where this scandal begins moving toward something astonishing.
Tamar conceived twins.
Perez and Zerah.
Perez became part of the line of Judah.
Generations passed.
Names became genealogies.
Families became nations.
Kings came.
And then Matthew opened his Gospel with a genealogy that ancient public-relations consultants probably would have edited.
Abraham.
Isaac.
Jacob.
Judah.
And then—
Tamar.
Matthew 1:3 deliberately remembers her:
“Judah the father of Perez and Zerah by Tamar.”
Her name survived the scandal.
More than that.
Her story became part of the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
Think about what that means carefully.
The Gospel is not saying the Messiah needed sin.
God is never the author of evil.
The Gospel is showing something far more glorious:
Human sin cannot derail God’s redemptive purpose.
God does not need a spotless human family tree to send a spotless Savior.
Jesus entered a genealogy filled with broken people because He came to save broken people.
Tamar appears there.
Rahab appears there.
Ruth appears there.
David appears there, with Matthew deliberately reminding us of “the wife of Uriah.”
The genealogy refuses cosmetic surgery.
Then comes Jesus.
Not another compromised man.
Not another sinner requiring redemption.
The Redeemer Himself.
The sinless Son of God.
The One who would eventually stand before another condemned woman while religious men prepared to weaponize her shame.
The One who touched people respectable society avoided.
The One who ate with sinners.
The One who exposed hypocrites.
The One who welcomed repentant outcasts.
The One who carried our shame to a Roman cross.
The One who was stripped so sinners could be clothed in righteousness.
The One who was condemned though innocent so guilty people could be forgiven.
This is Christianity.
Not pretending your family tree has no Tamar.
Not pretending your hands contain no evidence.
Not pretending your past never happened.
Christianity begins when sinners stop defending themselves and come to Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have spent years thinking the ugliest thing that happened to you disqualified you.
Maybe what somebody did to you still whispers that you are damaged goods.
Maybe what you did still follows you into worship.
Maybe you have become Judah, suddenly recognizing evidence of your own hypocrisy.
Maybe you have been Tamar, waiting while people with more power determined what happened next.
Maybe, if you are painfully honest, you have been both wounded and wounder.
Most of us have.
That is why we need more than inspiration.
We need a Savior.
Jesus does not merely improve scandalous people.
He raises spiritually dead people to life.
He does not merely teach us to manage shame.
At the cross, He deals with guilt.
He does not tell us repentance is unnecessary because our pain explains everything.
He calls us to repentance because His grace is powerful enough to forgive everything we genuinely bring to Him.
Repentance is not paying Jesus back.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the Savior who already paid what you could never pay.
The cross says your sin is worse than your excuses admit.
And the cross simultaneously says His grace is greater than your shame can imagine.
That is why nobody reading this should use Tamar’s story to justify sin.
And nobody should use Tamar’s story to imprison a repentant sinner forever inside a past Jesus has forgiven.
The Gospel does neither.
It tells the truth.
Then grace enters the truth.
Perhaps you have been hiding.
Stop hiding.
Jesus already knows.
Perhaps you have been blaming everybody else.
Come into the light.
Jesus already knows.
Perhaps somebody’s betrayal convinced you God abandoned you.
Look again at Tamar.
Human beings were making decisions.
God was still writing history.
People saw a widow waiting in her father’s house.
God saw generations.
People saw scandal.
God saw a lineage through which, according to the flesh, the Messiah would eventually come.
People saw a woman whose future seemed suspended.
God had not lost the thread.
And if you belong to Christ, He has not lost yours.
That does not mean every earthly wound will receive the ending you wanted.
It does not mean every marriage will be restored, every betrayer will apologize, every stolen year will return, or every consequence will disappear.
Biblical hope is stronger than fantasy.
Our ultimate hope is Jesus Himself.
Forgiveness in Him.
Reconciliation with God through Him.
A new identity in Him.
Resurrection because of Him.
Eternal life with Him.
And transformation through His Spirit beginning now.
So be honest.
Did this story expose something?
Did you recognize Tamar’s waiting?
Judah’s hypocrisy?
Onan’s selfishness?
Or perhaps something in yourself you have been trying not to name?
Respond to God.
If you need repentance, repent.
If you need forgiveness, ask Christ for mercy.
If you have never trusted Jesus Christ, come to Him.
He died for sinners and rose again.
You do not clean yourself enough to approach Him.
You come because you cannot save yourself.
And if you have spent too long pretending everything is fine, maybe today your confession is simply:
“No more hiding.”
Not because a comment saves you.
Jesus saves.
But sometimes publicly admitting that you need prayer is the first crack in a wall you have spent years constructing.
And somebody reading your comment may realize they are not fighting alone.
Not merely because you enjoyed it.
Someone may need to discover that the Bible does not hide broken families.
Someone may need to hear that Jesus Christ still receives repentant sinners.
Someone may be one honest encounter with the Gospel away from coming home.
There may come a night when shame starts speaking again, and you need to remember that Tamar’s name did not disappear in Genesis 38.
It appeared again in Matthew 1.
Stay close to daily Scripture, biblical conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and truth centered on Jesus Christ.
It does not.
Not because giving money purchases blessing.
It cannot.
We should never manipulate people by suggesting that God is more pleased with paying supporters than with those who cannot afford to give.
We glorify God through faith in Christ expressed in obedience, love, generosity, truth, and service.
But supporting Gospel work can be one practical expression of that generosity.
Christ cannot be purchased.
Salvation is the gift of God received through faith in Jesus Christ.
So pray.
Repent.
Forgive.
Seek Christ.
Open your Bible.
Tell someone about Jesus.
Share truth.
Carry somebody else’s burden.
And remember Tamar.
The woman sent away to wait.
The woman whose future appeared to rest in the hands of men.
The woman standing inside one of Scripture’s most uncomfortable scandals.
Her name survived.
Her story continued.
And generations later, when Matthew began telling the world about Jesus Christ, there she was.
Tamar.
Because God is not embarrassed by the places where His grace demonstrates just how desperately humanity needs redemption.
Maybe people have already written the final sentence over your life.
Maybe you wrote it yourself.
Failure.
Ruined.
Unwanted.
Unclean.
Too late.
Too complicated.
Too far gone.
But if you are still breathing, you do not get to call the story finished while Jesus Christ is still calling sinners to Himself.
Come into the light.
Bring Him the truth.
Bring Him the grief.
Bring Him the sin.
Bring Him the shame.
Bring Him the years you cannot recover.
And surrender all of it to the Savior who died and rose again.
Because the most unforgettable thing about Tamar is not simply that she survived a scandal.
It is that the scandal could not prevent God from carrying His redemptive promise forward until history reached Jesus.
What people treated like the end of Tamar’s story, God placed inside the genealogy of the Savior.
